rows.text:
The main steps of an IVF cycle are:

1. Stimulating the ovaries so several eggs mature.
2. Egg retrieval (egg collection).
3. Fertilising the eggs in the laboratory.
4. Transferring an embryo into the uterus.

There are also monitoring scans and blood tests, a trigger injection before egg collection

rows.text: One IVF cycle usually takes several weeks. Stimulation lasts about 1 to 2 weeks, embryos develop in the lab for 2 to 6 days, and the pregnancy test is done roughly two weeks after embryo transfer. Your clinic will give you your own calendar with exact dates [1].

rows.text: An antral follicle count (AFC) is an ultrasound scan that counts the small follicles in your ovaries. Along with the AMH test, it helps predict whether you might have a low or high response to ovarian stimulation during IVF [1][2].

rows.text: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is tested on day 3 of your cycle because its level at this time gives information about your ovarian reserve. High day-3 FSH can suggest lower ovarian reserve, but a normal result does not rule it out [1].

rows.q: What is ovarian reserve?
top3: Ovarian reserve and age
Ovarian reserve and age
Ovarian reserve and age
rows.text: Ovarian reserve describes the number (and broadly the quality) of eggs remaining in your ovaries. People are born with all their eggs, and the number declines over time—slowly until the early 30s, then more quickly after the mid-30s [1].

rows.text: Fertility declines with age. For healthy couples in their 20s or early 30s, the chance of pregnancy is about 25–30% per cycle. rows.text: Pituitary suppression is when medicines are used to temporarily quieten your natural hormone signals from the pituitary gland. This helps your care team control when your eggs mature during IVF treatment, making the process more predictable and improving the chances of collecting multiple eggs [1].

During IVF, the main groups of medicines used are:

- Gonadotropin injections (FSH, sometimes with LH) to grow several follicles (eggs)
- GnRH agonists or antagonists to prevent early ovulation
- A trigger injection (hCG or a GnRH agonist) to finish egg maturation before egg collection

cited: IVF medications and common side effects
rows.text: Common side effects of fertility injections include bloating, breast tenderness, mood changes, headaches, tiredness, and bruising or soreness at injection sites. Mild ovarian hyperstimulation symptoms, such as bloating and nausea, can also occur [1].

rows.text: You need several monitoring scans and blood tests during stimulation to check how your follicles are growing and how your body is responding to the medication. This helps your care team adjust your treatment if needed, make sure your eggs grow at the right speed, and reduce risks like ovarian hypers

The trigger injection
cited: Monitoring scans and blood tests during stimulation
rows.text: Follicles are usually ready for the trigger injection when they are about 18–20 mm in size. Your care team decides the exact timing based on your scans and blood tests [1].

rows.q: What does the trigger shot do?
top3: The trigger injection
The trigger injection
Trigger injection and egg collection
rows.text: The trigger shot helps the eggs finish maturing so they can be collected. It is given at a very specific time, and egg collection is usually done about 36 hours later. The timing is important to make sure the eggs are ready but not released before collection [2][3].

rows.q: Why is the timing of the trigger injection so important?
top3: The trigger injection
Trigger injection and egg collection
The trigger injection
rows.text: The timing of the trigger injection is very important because it helps the eggs finish maturing so they can be collected at the right moment. Egg collection is scheduled about 36 hours after the trigger. If the timing is off, the eggs may not be mature enough or could be released before collection,

rows.text: During egg retrieval, you are given sedation or pain relief. The procedure usually takes about 15 to 30 minutes, and you usually go home

Egg retrieval (egg collection): what happens
rows.text: After egg collection, it’s common to have cramping, mild bleeding, and bloating for a day or two. These symptoms usually improve quickly. If you experience severe pain, heavy bleeding, fever, fainting, or difficulty breathing, contact your care team right away [1].

rows.text: OHSS (ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome) is a possible reaction to fertility medications. It happens when the ovaries respond too strongly, causing many follicles and high hormone levels. rows.text:
Warning signs of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) include:

- Severe abdominal pain or swelling
- Vomiting or being unable to keep fluids down
- Shortness of breath
- Passing little urine
- Rapid weight gain

If you notice any of these symptoms, contact your clinic urgently or seek emergency

rows.q: How can OHSS be prevented?

cited: OHSS (ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome): symptoms, warning signs and prevention
rows.text: OHSS can be reduced by using lower stimulation doses, certain medications (like an agonist trigger or cabergoline), and sometimes by freezing all embryos instead of doing a fresh transfer. These strategies help lower the risk of developing OHSS during IVF treatment [1].

rows.text:
The main difference is how the egg is fertilised:

- In IVF, eggs and many sperm are placed together in the lab, and fertilisation happens naturally.
- In ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection), a single sperm is injected directly into each mature egg.

The rest of the process—stimulation, egg coll

rows.q: When is ICSI used?
top3: IVF compared with ICSI

rows.text: ICSI is mainly used for male factor infertility, such as low sperm count, poor sperm movement or shape, when sperm is surgically retrieved, or if fertilisation failed in a previous IVF cycle. Your care team will advise if ICSI is right for your situation [1][3][4].

rows.text: The day after insemination or ICSI, the embryologist checks your eggs for signs of fertilisation. They look for two pronuclei (one from the egg, one from the sperm), which confirms fertilisation has happened. Usually, about 65% to 75% of mature eggs fertilise, but this can vary [1][3].

rows.q: What is a blastocyst?

rows.text: A blastocyst is an embryo that has developed a fluid-filled cavity and has distinct cells that will become the baby (inner cell mass) and the placenta (trophectoderm). This stage is usually reached about 5 days after egg retrieval. Not all embryos reach the blastocyst stage, which is normal [1].

An embryo grade like 4AA is a way to describe a blastocyst’s quality:

- The number (4) shows how expanded the blastocyst is.
- The first letter (A) grades the inner cell mass (the part that becomes the baby).
- The second letter (A) grades the trophectoderm (the part that becomes the placenta).

rows.text: PGT-M is used when there is a known risk of passing on a specific serious inherited single-gene condition. It helps select embryos that do not have that condition before transfer. IVF is needed even if there are no fertility problems, and embryos are usually frozen and transferred later [1][2].

rows.text: You should take a pregnancy test on the date your clinic gives you, which is usually about two weeks after embryo transfer. Testing early can give false results. Keep taking any medication your clinic prescribed until they tell you otherwise [1][2][3][4].

rows.text: During the two-week wait, it is normal to have cramping, spotting, breast tenderness, or no symptoms at all. These do not reliably show whether treatment has worked. Contact your clinic if you have heavy bleeding, severe pain, or symptoms of OHSS (ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome) [1].

rows.text: After egg collection, your body may not make enough progesterone to prepare the womb lining for pregnancy. Progesterone is usually given after IVF to help the womb get ready for an embryo to implant and support early pregnancy [1].

Luteal phase support (progesterone)
rows.text: Luteal phase support is the use of progesterone after egg collection in IVF. It helps prepare the womb lining for pregnancy because your body may not make enough progesterone on its own after the procedure [2].

rows.text: Yes, it is recommended that both partners stop smoking before IVF. Smoking can reduce fertility in women and lower sperm count and movement in men, which may affect IVF success [1].

The main risks of IVF include:

- Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS)
- Multiple pregnancy (twins or more)
- Ectopic pregnancy
- Miscarriage
- Small risks from egg collection, such as bleeding or infection

If you have any concerns or symptoms, please discuss them with your care team [1].
